Revitalize

/ree-VY-tl-eyez/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Revitalize means to bring new energy and strength back to something that has slowly grown weak, dull, or inactive.

Hoping to revitalize the diner's tired menu, the new chef added a dozen colorful dishes that soon had regulars lining up out the door again.

Worked Example

After weeks of drought, a single night of steady rain revitalized the tomato garden, and by morning the drooping vines stood tall and green again.

The vines had grown weak and droopy, and the rain gave them back their strength and liveliness overnight. Bringing fresh life and energy to something that was fading is exactly what revitalize means.

How Revitalize Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

rejuvenate

rejuvenate: to make something feel young and fresh again

reinvigorate

reinvigorate: to give new energy or strength to

refresh

refresh: to renew energy or interest

Antonyms

exhaust

exhaust: to drain completely of energy

deaden

deaden: to make dull or lifeless

How Strong Is It? — refresh → revitalize → resurrect

refresh vs. revitalize

refresh vs. revitalize: Refresh is weaker than revitalize; a cold drink refreshes you for a moment, but it does not give something whole new life.

resurrect vs. revitalize

resurrect vs. revitalize: Resurrect is stronger than revitalize; you revitalize something that is fading, but you resurrect something that is completely gone.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-

Prefix — re-: again, back

Root — vit

Root — vit: life (from Latin vita)

Suffix — -al

Suffix — -al: relating to

Suffix — -ize

Suffix — -ize: to make (verb-forming)

Put it together

Put it together: Re- means again, vit means life, and the endings -al and -ize turn the idea into an action verb. So revitalize literally means to make something full of life again.

Use the root in a new word: vitality

Use the root in a new word: vitality: The old dog surprised everyone with the vitality of a puppy the moment the leash came off the hook.

Root Check

Word Choice

Neutral / journalistic

Common in news writing about places and institutions: people revitalize a downtown, an economy, or a career. Do not confuse it with revive, which often means bringing someone back to consciousness; revitalize means pumping fresh energy into something that still exists but has gone flat.
